q: To collect on a property policy, an insured must have an insurable interest:
o: At the time of the loss
Only when the policy is applied for
At both application and 10 years after the loss
Never; it applies only to life insurance
x: In property insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss. In life insurance, it must exist at the time of application.
k: Property: insurable interest at time of loss.

q: Actual cash value is most commonly calculated as:
o: The amount stated on the application
x: Actual cash value is usually replacement cost at the time of loss minus physical depreciation. Some courts use fair market value or the broad evidence rule.

q: A 10-year-old roof with a 20-year expected life is destroyed. Replacement cost is $12,000. What is the actual cash value?
Which valuation method pays to repair or replace with materials of like kind and quality without deducting depreciation?
x: Replacement cost pays the current cost to repair or replace with like kind and quality, without depreciation. Functional replacement cost uses modern, less expensive materials that perform the same function.

q: An older home has ornate plaster walls. The policy pays to replace them with drywall that serves the same purpose. This valuation is:
x: Functional replacement cost uses modern, less expensive materials that are functionally equivalent. It is common for older homes whose market value is well below reproduction cost.
k: Functionally equivalent, cheaper materials = functional replacement cost.

q: A fine art collector and insurer agree in advance that a painting is worth $80,000, and that amount will be paid for a total loss. This is:
x: Agreed value is set when the policy is written and paid in full for a total loss, without depreciation. It is common for art and collectibles.
k: Value fixed in advance = agreed value.

q: A "stated amount" policy on a classic car differs from an agreed value policy because it pays:
o: The lesser of the stated amount, ACV, or cost to repair or replace
The stated amount in every total loss
More than the stated amount if values rise
x: A stated amount is a maximum, not a guarantee. The insurer pays the lesser of the stated amount, actual cash value, or repair or replacement cost.
k: Stated amount = a ceiling, not a promise.

q: Named perils coverage differs from special (open perils) coverage because named perils coverage:
o: Covers only losses caused by perils specifically listed
Covers all losses unless specifically excluded
Requires the insurer to prove an exclusion applies
x: Named perils covers only listed perils, and the insured must show a listed peril caused the loss. Special (open perils) covers direct physical loss unless excluded, and the insurer must show an exclusion applies.
k: Named = listed only. Open = all except excluded.

q: After a fire, a restaurant loses income while closed for repairs. This lost income is a:
x: A direct loss is physical damage to property. Lost income, extra expense, and spoilage that result from that damage are consequential or indirect losses.
k: Lost income after damage = indirect loss.

q: One limit that applies to several buildings or locations together is called:
x: Blanket insurance applies one limit across multiple items or locations. Specific insurance assigns a separate limit to each item or location.
k: One limit over many items = blanket.

q: Which construction type is generally the most fire-resistive?
x: Fire-resistive construction has the best fire rating. Frame is the most combustible, and unprotected steel can weaken in high heat.
k: Frame is worst; fire-resistive is best.

q: A building's value is $400,000 and the policy has an 80% coinsurance clause. What is the minimum amount of insurance required to avoid a coinsurance penalty?
x: Required insurance = value × coinsurance percentage = $400,000 × 80% = $320,000.

q: A building worth $500,000 is insured for $300,000 with an 80% coinsurance clause. A $100,000 loss occurs and there is no deductible. What does the insurer pay?
A building worth $200,000 is insured for $160,000 with an 80% coinsurance clause and a $1,000 deductible. A $50,000 loss occurs. What does the insurer pay?
x: Required = $200,000 × 80% = $160,000, so the insured met coinsurance. Payment = $50,000 − $1,000 deductible = $49,000.

q: A coinsurance penalty applies when:
o: The insured carries less than the required percentage of value at the time of loss
The loss is a total loss
The insured files more than one claim a year
x: Coinsurance is measured at the time of loss. If the limit is below the required percentage of value, partial losses are paid proportionally. Payment never exceeds the limit.
k: Underinsured at time of loss = penalty.

q: Two policies cover the same building: Insurer A for $60,000 and Insurer B for $40,000. Under a pro rata other-insurance clause, how much does A pay on a $20,000 loss?
k: Pro rata = each pays its share of total limits.

q: Under contribution by equal shares, two insurers with limits of $50,000 and $200,000 cover a $150,000 loss. How much does each pay?
o: $50,000 from the first and $100,000 from the second
x: Each pays equally until the smaller limit is used up: $50,000 each ($100,000). The remaining $50,000 comes from the second insurer, for $100,000 total from it.
k: Equal shares until the smaller limit runs out.

q: After paying a claim, the insurer takes over the insured's right to recover from the party who caused the loss. This is:
x: Subrogation transfers the insured's recovery rights against a responsible third party to the insurer, to the extent the insurer paid. It prevents the insured from collecting twice.
k: Insurer steps into insured's shoes = subrogation.

q: An insurer pays a total loss on a stolen motorcycle, then the motorcycle is recovered. Taking and selling the motorcycle is the insurer's right of:
x: Salvage is damaged or recovered property the insurer takes after paying the claim. The abandonment clause says the insured cannot simply abandon property to the insurer without its agreement.
k: Insurer keeps recovered or damaged property = salvage.

q: The abandonment provision in a property policy means:
o: The insured cannot abandon damaged property to the insurer and demand full payment
The insurer may abandon the insured after a claim
The insured may abandon the policy at any time without notice
x: The insurer need not accept property the insured abandons. The insurer decides whether to take salvage.
k: You can't dump damaged property on the insurer.

q: The liberalization clause provides that:
o: If the insurer broadens a form without extra premium, the broader coverage applies automatically to existing policies
The insurer may reduce coverage at any time
The insured may add coverage without paying
Claims will be paid faster after a catastrophe
x: Under liberalization, broadened coverage adopted without extra premium during the policy term (or a set period before it) automatically applies to existing policies.

q: Which part of a property policy lists the named insured, address, limits, premium, and policy period?
x: The declarations page summarizes the who, what, where, when, and how much of the policy.

q: Which part of a policy states the insurer's promise to pay?
x: The insuring agreement states what the insurer promises to cover. Conditions state the duties of both parties, and exclusions remove coverage.
k: The promise to pay = insuring agreement.

q: When a policy has several named insureds, cancellation requests and premium payments are usually the responsibility of the:
x: The first named insured, listed first on the declarations, is responsible for premium payments and receiving return premiums, and is the party that may request cancellation.
k: First named insured handles premium and cancellation.

q: After a covered loss, a property policy's "duties after loss" condition requires the insured to:
o: Give prompt notice, protect the property from further damage, and provide a proof of loss if asked
Wait 30 days before reporting the loss
Repair the property before the adjuster inspects
Admit liability to any third party
x: Typical duties include prompt notice, protecting property from further damage, keeping records, showing the damaged property, and giving a signed, sworn proof of loss if requested.

q: A loss payable clause is most commonly used to protect:
o: A lender with an interest in personal property, such as a financed car or equipment
A neighbor injured on the premises
A contractor working on the building
x: The loss payable clause adds a secured creditor on personal property as a payee. The standard mortgage clause is used for real property.
k: Loss payable = lender on personal property.

q: The "no benefit to bailee" provision means:
o: A party holding the insured's property for a fee cannot benefit from the insured's coverage
The insured cannot recover for property left with others
The insurer will not subrogate against a bailee
A bailee's customers are automatically covered
x: No benefit to bailee prevents a bailee, such as a dry cleaner or repair shop, from avoiding responsibility by relying on the owner's insurance. This preserves the insurer's subrogation rights.
k: Bailee can't use the owner's insurance to escape liability.

q: A loss ratio is calculated as:
o: Losses (incurred losses and loss adjustment expense) divided by earned premium
Claims count divided by policy count
x: The loss ratio compares losses to premiums. A high loss ratio signals rates may be inadequate or underwriting too loose.

q: The dwelling policy (DP) program is most often used to insure:
o: Owner-occupied or rental dwellings that are not eligible for, or do not need, a homeowners policy
x: Dwelling forms cover residential structures of one to four units, including rentals, seasonal homes, and homes that do not qualify for homeowners coverage.

q: The DP-1 (Basic Form) covers which perils without optional endorsements?
o: All risks of direct physical loss
x: The DP-1 covers fire, lightning, and internal explosion. Extended coverage perils and vandalism or malicious mischief can be added for an additional premium.

q: Which dwelling form covers the dwelling and other structures on an open perils (special) basis?
x: The DP-3 covers Coverages A and B against open perils and personal property against broad named perils. The DP-2 is broad named perils and the DP-1 is basic named perils.

q: In the dwelling policy, Coverage D provides:
x: Dwelling Coverage D is fair rental value (lost rent). Coverage E is additional living expense. Liability requires the personal liability supplement.
k: DP Cov D = fair rental value; Cov E = ALE.

q: Which dwelling coverage is NOT included in the DP-1 basic form?
x: The DP-1 includes Coverages A, B, C, and D. Additional living expense (Coverage E) is included in the DP-2 and DP-3.

q: How does a landlord insured under a dwelling policy get coverage for tenants' injuries caused by the landlord's negligence?
o: It is automatically included in Coverage A
Buy a DP-3 instead of a DP-1
Liability coverage is not available for rentals
x: Dwelling forms are property-only. The personal liability supplement adds personal liability and medical payments to others.
k: DP liability comes from the personal liability supplement.

q: Under the dwelling forms, other structures coverage is provided as an additional amount equal to what percentage of the Coverage A limit?
x: The dwelling forms let the insured use up to 10% of the Coverage A limit for other structures, in addition to Coverage A.

q: Which endorsement adds theft coverage to a dwelling policy?
x: Standard dwelling forms do not cover theft of personal property. The broad theft coverage endorsement (DP 04 72) adds it for owner-occupied dwellings.

q: The automatic increase in insurance endorsement (DP 04 11) is used to:
o: Increase Coverage A by an annual percentage to keep up with rising construction costs
Automatically double limits after a loss
Add replacement cost to personal property
x: The automatic increase endorsement raises the Coverage A limit gradually during the policy term by a selected annual percentage.

q: Which endorsement is used when a dwelling is being built?
x: The dwelling under construction endorsement adjusts the limit to reflect the increasing value of a residence under construction.
k: Building a house on a DP = DP 11 43.

q: Under the dwelling policy, an insured dwelling that has been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days generally loses coverage for:
x: Vandalism, malicious mischief, and glass breakage are excluded once a building has been vacant more than 60 consecutive days. Fire and lightning coverage continues.

q: Which peril is a general exclusion in the dwelling forms?
x: General exclusions include flood and surface water, earth movement, ordinance or law, war, nuclear hazard, neglect, and intentional loss.
k: Flood and earth movement are excluded.

q: Which dwelling form covers personal property against broad named perils rather than basic perils?
o: The DP-3 only, on an open perils basis
x: The DP-2 covers the building and contents on a broad named perils basis. The DP-3 covers the building on an open perils basis and contents on a broad named perils basis.
k: DP-2 and DP-3 contents = broad named perils.

q: A dwelling policy loss settlement on the dwelling is on a replacement cost basis under which forms?
x: The DP-1 settles at actual cash value. The DP-2 and DP-3 use replacement cost for the dwelling and other structures when insurance-to-value requirements are met.

q: Which homeowners form is designed for renters?
x: The HO-4 (Contents Broad Form) covers a tenant's personal property, loss of use, and liability. It has no dwelling coverage.

q: Which homeowners form is designed for condominium unit owners?
x: The HO-6 covers a condo owner's personal property, the owner's building items and improvements (Coverage A), loss of use, and liability.

q: Which homeowners form is used for older homes whose replacement cost greatly exceeds market value?
x: The HO-8 is for homes where replacement cost is much higher than market value. It generally settles losses using functional replacement cost or actual cash value and covers basic named perils.
k: Old home, RC far above market value = HO-8.

q: Under the HO-3, the dwelling (Coverage A) is covered on what basis?
x: The HO-3 covers Coverages A and B against open perils, and Coverage C against broad named perils.
k: HO-3 = open perils on dwelling, named perils on contents.

q: Under an unendorsed HO-3, personal property (Coverage C) is covered against:
x: Coverage C in the HO-3 is named perils, the same broad list used in the HO-2. The HO-5 or an endorsement is needed for open perils on contents.

q: Under an HO-3 with a Coverage A limit of $300,000, what is the Coverage B (other structures) limit?
x: Coverage B equals 10% of Coverage A: $300,000 × 10% = $30,000.

q: Under an HO-3 with a Coverage A limit of $300,000, what is the Coverage C (personal property) limit?
x: Coverage C equals 50% of Coverage A: $300,000 × 50% = $150,000.

q: Under an HO-3, the Coverage D (loss of use) limit equals what percentage of Coverage A?
x: On the HO-2 and HO-3, Coverage D equals 30% of Coverage A. It includes additional living expense and fair rental value.

q: Under the HO-3 replacement cost loss settlement, the insurer pays full replacement cost for a covered dwelling loss (up to the limit) when the Coverage A limit is at least what percentage of the dwelling's replacement cost at the time of loss?
x: If Coverage A is at least 80% of full replacement cost, the insurer pays replacement cost without deduction for depreciation, up to the limit. If not, it pays the greater of ACV or a proportion of replacement cost.

q: Homeowners Section II includes which two coverages?
o: Coverage E – Personal liability and Coverage F – Medical payments to others
Coverage A – Dwelling and Coverage B – Other structures
Coverage C – Personal property and Coverage D – Loss of use
x: Section I covers property (A through D). Section II covers personal liability (E) and medical payments to others (F).
k: Section II = E (liability) + F (med pay to others).

q: Homeowners Coverage F (medical payments to others) does NOT pay for injuries to:
o: The named insured or regular household residents
A guest injured on the premises
A delivery person bitten by the insured's dog
A neighbor injured by the insured's golf ball away from the premises
x: Medical payments to others pays regardless of fault for injuries to others, not to the insured or regular household members (other than residence employees).
k: Med pay to others excludes the insured's household.

q: What is the standard minimum Coverage E personal liability limit on a homeowners policy?
x: The basic homeowners liability limit is $100,000 per occurrence, and it can be increased.

q: Under the HO-3's special limits of liability, theft of jewelry, watches, and furs is limited to:
x: The HO special limits include $200 for money, $1,500 for theft of jewelry and furs, and $2,500 for theft of firearms and silverware. Higher values are scheduled with the scheduled personal property endorsement.

q: Under the HO-3's special limits of liability, money and bank notes are limited to:
x: Money, bank notes, and similar items carry a $200 special limit. Securities and valuable papers are limited to $1,500.

q: A homeowner wants full coverage for a $12,000 engagement ring, including mysterious disappearance. The best solution is:
o: The personal property replacement cost endorsement (HO 04 90)
x: Scheduling the ring removes the theft sublimit and provides broad coverage on the scheduled item, usually without a deductible.

q: The personal property replacement cost endorsement (HO 04 90) changes Coverage C loss settlement from:
o: Actual cash value to replacement cost
Replacement cost to actual cash value
x: Unendorsed homeowners forms settle personal property at ACV. HO 04 90 changes that to replacement cost.

q: Earthquake damage to a home is excluded under the HO-3 unless:
x: Earth movement is excluded. The earthquake endorsement adds the coverage, usually with a percentage deductible.

q: Water that backs up through a basement floor drain is excluded under an unendorsed HO-3. Which endorsement adds this coverage?
o: Water back-up and sump discharge or overflow (HO 04 95)
x: Sewer and drain back-up and sump overflow are excluded. The HO 04 95 endorsement adds limited coverage.

q: An insured runs a licensed day care business from her home. What should her agent recommend?
o: The home day care endorsement (HO 04 97) or a separate commercial policy
Nothing; homeowners covers home businesses automatically
x: Business pursuits, including home day care, are largely excluded under homeowners Section II. The home day care endorsement or a commercial policy is needed.
k: Home day care = HO 04 97 or commercial coverage.

q: Which is excluded under homeowners Section II (liability)?
o: Bodily injury the insured expected or intended
Injury to a guest who slips on an icy sidewalk
Damage caused by the insured's child breaking a neighbor's window
A golf ball hitting another golfer
x: Section II excludes expected or intended injury, business pursuits, professional services, most motor vehicles, and injury to insureds, among others. Accidental injuries to others are covered.

q: Mold damage under the HO-3 is generally excluded except for limited coverage that can be provided by:
o: The limited fungi, wet or dry rot, or bacteria endorsement (HO 04 26/HO 04 27)
The personal property replacement cost endorsement
x: Fungi, wet or dry rot, and bacteria are excluded. The limited fungi endorsements provide specified limits of coverage.

q: Which peril is covered under the HO-2 broad form but NOT under a basic named perils form?
x: Broad form adds perils such as falling objects; weight of ice, snow, or sleet; accidental discharge of water or steam; freezing; and sudden and accidental damage from artificially generated electrical current.
k: Broad adds falling objects, weight of ice/snow, freezing, water discharge.

q: Under the HO-3, how are trees, shrubs, and plants covered?
o: As an additional coverage for named perils, with a per-item limit, not including windstorm
Under Coverage A on an open perils basis
x: Trees, shrubs, and plants are an additional coverage for specified perils (not windstorm), subject to a per-tree limit and an overall percentage of Coverage A.
k: Trees: additional coverage, named perils, no wind.

q: Under homeowners policies, the vacancy exclusion for vandalism and malicious mischief applies after the dwelling has been vacant for more than:
x: Vandalism, malicious mischief, and glass breakage coverage is excluded if the dwelling has been vacant more than 60 consecutive days before the loss.

q: Which statement about watercraft under an unendorsed homeowners policy is correct?
o: Section II covers some small boats, but larger or higher-horsepower boats need a watercraft endorsement or boatowners policy
All boats are fully covered under Section I and Section II
Watercraft is covered only while on the insured's premises
x: Section II excludes liability for many owned watercraft above certain size and horsepower thresholds, and Section I has a low special limit for watercraft. Larger boats need an endorsement or a boatowners policy.
k: Bigger boats need an endorsement or boat policy.

q: Under homeowners Section I, the deductible generally applies:
o: Per occurrence to Section I property losses
x: The homeowners deductible applies per occurrence to Section I property losses. It does not apply to Section II liability or medical payments.

q: Flood insurance is available through the National Flood Insurance Program only when:
o: The property is in a community that participates in the NFIP
The property is in a high-risk flood zone only
x: NFIP coverage is available in participating communities, which agree to adopt floodplain management rules. It is available in and outside high-risk zones.

q: New NFIP flood policies generally have a waiting period before coverage takes effect of:
x: Most new NFIP policies have a 30-day waiting period. Exceptions include coverage bought in connection with making, increasing, or renewing a loan.

q: What is the maximum NFIP building coverage for a single-family residence?
x: The NFIP residential limits are $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for contents. Excess flood coverage is available in the private market.

q: Under the NFIP "Write Your Own" program:
o: Private insurers issue and service flood policies under their own names, with the federal government bearing the risk
Homeowners write their own flood policy terms
Only FEMA may sell flood coverage
Agents may change NFIP policy terms
x: In the WYO program, participating private insurers sell and service NFIP policies, while the federal program underwrites the risk. Coverage terms are the same as direct NFIP policies.
k: WYO = private insurer sells; government takes the risk.

q: A family wants coverage for its 24-foot boat with a 200-horsepower engine, including liability. The best choice is:
x: Homeowners forms give very limited watercraft property coverage and exclude liability for larger boats. A boatowners policy provides hull, equipment, and liability coverage.

q: A mobile home policy is generally written:
o: As a homeowners-type form adapted for manufactured homes at a fixed location
x: Manufactured and mobile homes are generally insured on homeowners-type forms adapted by endorsement or a separate program, covering the home, contents, and liability.
k: Mobile homes use adapted homeowners-type coverage.

q: Earthquake insurance typically uses which type of deductible?
o: A percentage of the dwelling's limit
A deductible equal to one year's premium
x: Earthquake coverage usually has a percentage deductible, such as 5% to 20% of the Coverage A limit, because losses can be catastrophic.

q: Directors and officers (D&O) liability insurance protects:
o: Directors and officers against claims alleging wrongful acts in managing the organization
x: D&O covers claims of wrongful acts, such as mismanagement or breach of duty, against directors and officers. Many D&O policies also reimburse the organization when it indemnifies them.

q: Which statement about NFIP flood coverage for a basement is correct?
o: Coverage for basement contents and improvements is limited
Basement contents are covered in full
Basements are covered only for sewer backup
x: NFIP coverage in basements is restricted: it covers certain building items and equipment, and many contents and finished improvements are not covered.

q: Which peril is excluded under standard homeowners forms and handled by the NFIP?
x: Flood and surface water are excluded under homeowners and dwelling forms. The NFIP and private flood insurers fill the gap.

q: An NFIP-defined flood generally requires:
o: A general and temporary condition of inundation of normally dry land affecting two or more acres or two or more properties
Any water damage in the home
Rain entering through a broken window
x: The NFIP definition requires a general and temporary inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties, or mudflow. A burst pipe is not a flood.
